title: Gradients of linear and quadratic forms

sections.body_md:
Several functions in optimization are built from a constant vector and a constant matrix. Their gradients have short formulas, and the formulas are easier to remember after one differentiation in coordinates.

A linear form \(c^{T} x\) has gradient \(c\). The squared Euclidean length \(\lVert x \rVert^2 = x^{T} x\) has gradient \(2x\). A quadratic form \(x^{T} A x\) is more careful. If \(A\) is not symmetric, each of \(x\) on the left and \(x\) on the right contributes, and the gradient is \((A + A^{T}) x\). If \(A\) is symmetric, \(A + A^{T} = 2A\), and the gradient collapses to \(2 A x\).

The squared residual \(\lVert A x - b \rVert^2\) is a composition. The residual is linear, the outer function is a squared length, and the chain rule produces \(2 A^{T}(A x - b)\). The transpose sits on \(A\) because the Jacobian of \(x \mapsto A x\) is \(A\), and the scalar chain rule transposes it.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(c\), \(b\), and \(A\) constant,
\[
\nabla (c^{T} x) = c, \qquad \nabla \lVert x \rVert^2 = 2x, \qquad \nabla (x^{T} A x) = (A + A^{T}) x.
\]
When \(A\) is symmetric, \(\nabla (\tfrac12 x^{T} A x + b^{T} x) = A x + b\), and the Hessian is \(A\). For a residual,
\[
\nabla \lVert A x - b \rVert^2 = 2 A^{T} (A x - b).
\]
The Hessian of \(x^{T} A x\) is \(A + A^{T}\), which is symmetric even when \(A\) is not.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A linear form with data (9, -2) has gradient \((9, -2)\), at every point. For a nonsymmetric quadratic, take \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 8 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\[
A + A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
At \((4, 8)\) the product \((A + A^{T}) x\) equals \((72, 36)\). Expanding the form gives \(9 x y\), whose partial derivatives \(9y\) and \(9x\) equal 72 and 36 at that point. The symmetric shortcut \(2 A x\) would have used the wrong matrix: \(2 A (4, 8) = 2(64, 4) = (128, 8)\), which matches neither partial derivative.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The factor \(2 A x\) is not the gradient of \(x^{T} A x\) unless \(A\) is symmetric. Replacing \(A\) by its symmetric part first, or using \(A + A^{T}\), is the repair. The residual gradient carries \(A^{T}\) on the left of the residual, not \(A\). The Hessian of a linear form is zero, not the identity. A one-half in front of a symmetric quadratic cancels the 2 in the gradient and leaves \(A x\), so dropping or keeping that one half changes the formula.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Minimizing \(\tfrac12 x^{T} A x + b^{T} x\) with symmetric \(A\) is the linear equation \(A x + b = 0\), and positive definiteness of \(A\) decides uniqueness. The second-order convexity test reads the same Hessian. Least squares is the residual case, with normal equations built from \(A^{T} A\).
